Theme

republic noun

also the Republic, Roman Republic, republican

classical

Cic. Rep. 1.39: rēs pūblica rēs populī
Levi–Bini p. 54
M-O s.v. era

rēs pūblica, reī pūblicae f.

noun, fifth declension, with an adjective

a republic; the Roman Republic

Classically the state, whatever its constitution: for Cicero a kingdom is a rēs pūblica too (Rep. 1.42). It means a republic where the context sets it against kings, as Levi and Bini allow (p. 54), and in the names of states: annō sextō Reī Pūblicae Gallicae, in the sixth year of the French Republic (Desfontaines, 1798, in Morgan–Owens).

Other words

  • lībertās, lībertātis f. — liberty: a state free of kings

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Tac. Ann. 1.1: lībertātem et cōnsulātum L. Brūtus īnstituit; Cic. Phil. 6.19 (Lewis & Short)

    Lewis & Short: the political freedom of a people not under monarchical rule. To the Romans the end of the kings was the beginning of liberty.

  • populāris rēs pūblica — a republic, a state of the people

    noun phrase: rēs pūblica with the adjective populāris · also used · modern · Levi–Bini p. 54

    Levi and Bini’s phrase, with populāre imperium, for a republic as against a kingdom.

Examples

  • līberī jam hinc populī Rōmānī rēs pāce bellōque gestās, annuōs magistrātūs, imperiaque lēgum potentiōra quam hominum peragam

    from here on I shall tell the deeds of the Roman people, now free, in peace and war: their magistrates elected for a year, and the rule of laws stronger than the rule of menLiv. 2.1.1

See also democracy, state, government, king.
